brief.topic: RAG vs fine-tuning: which problem each actually solves
brief.audience: PMs and engineers choosing how to improve an LLM feature

coreInsight: Choose by what the model is missing: retrieval fixes missing or changing facts, fine-tuning fixes behaviour like format and tone, and a better prompt is the cheapest first test for both.

hooks.text: RAG or fine-tuning? Ask what’s missing.
hooks.notes: Turns a confusing technical debate into one diagnostic question the viewer can use in their next meeting.

hooks.text: Fine-tuning is the wrong fix for most knowledge gaps.
hooks.notes: Punchy, but 'most' is hard to back up and invites argument rather than learning.

hooks.text: Your model doesn’t need training. It needs the right page.
hooks.notes: Memorable but only covers the RAG half of the decision.

selectionRationale: Highest total (23/25) and the most honest: it promises a decision rule rather than declaring a winner, and the reel delivers the rule plus a third, cheaper option.

caption.opening: “Should we fine-tune?” is usually the wrong first question. Ask what the model is missing.
body: Missing knowledge (private docs, facts that change every week) → retrieval. Put the right page in front of the model at answer time.
Missing behaviour (a format, a house tone, a narrow skill) → fine-tuning can help.
Ignoring clear instructions → fix the prompt first. It’s the cheapest experiment, and many teams skip it.
Plenty of products end up using retrieval and fine-tuning together. Whichever you try, measure it on the same eval set before and after.

claims.text: Retrieval suits missing or frequently changing knowledge; fine-tuning suits behaviour such as format, tone or narrow skills; prompt changes are the cheapest first test.
